Automotive Production in Greece Disrupted Amid Ongoing Political Protest Blockade

ATHENS—Production and supply chains in Greece’s automotive sector have been thrown into turmoil this week following an ongoing occupation of key industry sites by protesters, amid escalating political tensions between Greece and a foreign state. The demonstrations, which began early Tuesday at several industrial zones near Thessaloniki and Piraeus, have led to the complete blockade of multiple vehicle assembly and import facilities.

Cars Motorcycles and Marine Engine Trade and Import Co SA confirmed that its main distribution center in Piraeus has been inaccessible since the early hours of Wednesday. “Our operations are at a standstill. We are unable to receive shipments or fulfill orders at this time,” a spokesperson told reporters. The company, which handles both automotive and marine engine imports, is now assessing the potential impact on its supply contracts and delivery timelines.

Protesters, some carrying banners referencing recent diplomatic disputes, have established barricades and prevented staff from entering the premises. Police have so far maintained a perimeter but have not moved to disperse the crowds. The government has described the situation as “highly sensitive,” with a senior official at the Ministry of Development stating, “We are working to ensure the safety of all personnel and to restore access to these critical economic assets as soon as possible.”

Industry analysts warn that the blockade is already affecting vehicle deliveries nationwide. “The automotive industry in Greece relies heavily on timely imports and just-in-time logistics,” said Panagiotis Lazaridis, an analyst at the Hellenic Automotive Review. “Even a few days of disruption can quickly result in shortages at dealerships and mounting backlogs for customers.”

The Hellenic Association of Automotive Importers and Dealers estimates that over 2,000 vehicles are currently held up at affected facilities, with further delays expected if the protest continues. “We urge all parties to seek a peaceful resolution. Prolonged interruptions will not only affect our members, but also consumers awaiting delivery of vehicles,” the association said in a statement.

Union representatives have called for calm and dialogue. “Workers are caught in the middle of a geopolitical dispute they had no part in creating,” noted Nikos Papadopoulos, regional secretary for the Automotive Workers Union.

As of Thursday morning, negotiations between government mediators and protest leaders had yet to yield a breakthrough. With the blockade now entering its third day, the Greek automotive industry faces growing uncertainty over when normal operations can resume.
